Meditations by Marcus Aurelius

items.text:
For if you once gain time and respite, you will more easily command yourself

The Enchiridion by Epictetus

For if you once gain time and respite, you will more easily command yourself

XXIII If you ever happen to turn your attention to externals, for the pleasure of anyone, be assured that you have ruined your scheme of life

XXXVII If you have assumed any character beyond your strength, you have both demeaned yourself ill in that and quitted one which you might have supported

And do you feel no shame in delivering up your own mind to any reviler, to be disconcerted and confounded?

But if you wish not to be disappointed in your desires, that is in your own power

For this reason all Roman Stoics apply metaphors and images derived from military life

Others assumed the philosophic way of life in order to escape into the sphere of Stoic freedom

But if you would at the same time not pay the one, and yet receive the other, you are unreasonable and foolish

items.title: Each gets what it desires, but the great state must learn to abase itself
items.text:
Each gets what it desires, but the great state must learn to abase itself

Tao Te Ching by Lao Tzu

Each gets what it desires, but the great state must learn to abase itself

To him by whom this harmony is known, (The secret of) the unchanging (Tao) is shown, And in the knowledge wisdom finds its throne

All life-increasing arts to evil turn; Where the mind makes the vital breath to burn, (False) is the strength, (and o'er it we should mourn.)

While his intelligence reaches in every direction, cannot he (appear to) be without knowledge?

The difficulty in governing the people arises from their having much knowledge

Or life or wealth, To which would you adhere?

Therefore the sage knows (these things) of himself, but does not parade (his knowledge); loves, but does not (appear to set a) value on, himself

If we could renounce our sageness and discard our wisdom, it would be better for the people a hundredfold

items.title: Ye seem to me lukewarm ones: but coldly floweth all deep knowledge
items.text:
Ye seem to me lukewarm ones: but coldly floweth all deep knowledge

Thus Spake Zarathustra by Friedrich Nietzsche

Ye seem to me lukewarm ones: but coldly floweth all deep knowledge

And if ye cannot be saints of knowledge, then, I pray you, be at least its warriors

And this also did I learn among them: the praiser doeth as if he gave back; in truth, however, he wanteth more to be given him!

But that I am fond of Wisdom, and often too fond, is because she remindeth me very strongly of Life!

And if man should yet learn to fly, alas!

But this art also must one learn: to HAVE a shell, and a fine appearance, and sagacious blindness!

Or is it this: To feed on the acorns and grass of knowledge, and for the sake of truth to suffer hunger of soul?

The man of knowledge must be able not only to love his enemies, but also to hate his friends

items.text:
Oh, young man, if you have inherited money, don’t regard it as a help

Acres of Diamonds by Russell Conwell

Oh, young man, if you have inherited money, don’t regard it as a help

He knew he did not know enough to teach, but was sure he could learn, so he bravely asked for the place

Study it wherever you choose--in business, in your profession, in your housekeeping, whatever your life, that one thing is the secret of success

An odd trait of his character is his love for fire

If you can honestly attain unto riches in Philadelphia, it is your Christian and godly duty to do so

Conwell does with it, it is illuminative of his character, his aims, his ability

He began his search, very properly to my mind, at the Mountains of the Moon

One line in this classic hits hard.

How to Live on 24 Hours a Day by Arnold Bennett

One line in this classic hits hard.

I cannot possibly allow you to scatter priceless pearls of time with such Oriental lavishness

On Liberty by John Stuart Mill

Is it necessary that some part of mankind should persist in error, to enable any to realise the truth?

The examinations, however, in the higher branches of knowledge should, I conceive, be entirely voluntary
